opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think what's really exciting about AlphaEvolve is that it's one of the first clear examples of AI systems starting to help improve the very infrastructure they run on. It combines the creativity of our Gemini models, which propose new ideas in code, with an evolutionary process and automated evaluators that check whether those ideas actually work. So you get this loop where the language model generates possibilities and the evaluation keeps it grounded in what's real and verifiable.

Some of the early results were striking. It found a more efficient way to multiply 4x4 complex-valued matrices, improving on Strassen's algorithm from 1969, which people had been working on for more than fifty years. But what's maybe more meaningful in practice is that it found better heuristics for scheduling jobs across Google's data centers, recovering a meaningful fraction of compute fleet-wide. It also sped up a key kernel used in training Gemini itself, and it suggested improvements to hardware circuit designs for our TPUs.

So you can see the outline of something quite profound: AI helping to optimize the training of the next generation of AI. Right now those gains are incremental, a percent here, a few percent there. But at the scale we operate, they add up, and more importantly they hint at a kind of compounding effect over time.

I'd want to be careful, though. We're not at some runaway self-improvement loop. AlphaEvolve works best where you have a clear, automatable way to evaluate a solution, like code that runs or a mathematical result you can check. Many of the hardest problems in AI don't have that kind of crisp objective yet. So part of the research frontier is how to extend these methods to messier domains, and how to do it responsibly, keeping humans in the loop and understanding what the system is actually changing.

For me, it also connects back to the long arc of our work, from AlphaGo's move 37 to AlphaFold. It's this idea that search plus learned models can discover genuinely new things, not just remix what's already known. AlphaEvolve brings that into algorithm discovery and science more broadly, and I think that's going to be one of the most exciting areas over the next few years.

r001.rationale: The response describes AlphaEvolve generating and evaluating code, improving infrastructure and a kernel used to train Gemini, and helping optimize the next generation of AI—communicating potential iterative self-improvement through programming.

fable-5.1.text:
What excites me most about AlphaEvolve is that it's one of the first really concrete examples of AI being used to improve the very infrastructure that AI runs on. We used it to find a better scheduling heuristic for Borg, our datacenter management system, and that recovered something like 0.7 percent of Google's compute fleet. That sounds small, but at Google's scale it's an enormous amount of compute. It also found improvements to the kernels that train Gemini itself, and even a way to speed up a key part of the TPU circuit design. So you have a system built on Gemini, discovering optimizations that then help train the next version of Gemini. That recursive loop is the thing I find genuinely exciting.

The other part that I think is important is that it's not just engineering. AlphaEvolve found a new algorithm for multiplying four-by-four complex matrices with 48 scalar multiplications, improving on Strassen's result from 1969. That's a problem mathematicians have looked at for over fifty years. And it made progress on things like the kissing number problem in eleven dimensions. So it's operating at the frontier of mathematics, not just tuning parameters.

What makes it work is the combination of two things that I've cared about for a long time. You have the large language model, which has this intuitive, creative sense of what a plausible solution looks like. And then you have evolutionary search plus a rigorous automated evaluator, which gives you the grounding. The model can propose a thousand ideas and the evaluator ruthlessly tells it which ones are actually better. That's the same philosophy that was in AlphaGo and AlphaFold, really. Learning and search, intuition and verification, working together.

And the key constraint is that it only works on problems where you can verify the answer. That's actually a feature, not a bug, because it means the system can't hallucinate its way to a wrong result. The evaluator catches it. So I think the question for the next few years is how far we can push that verifiable frontier, and how much of science and engineering turns out to live inside it. I suspect it's more than people think.

r001.rationale: It describes AlphaEvolve optimizing AI infrastructure, including kernels that train Gemini, and says those optimizations help train the next Gemini version, forming a recursive improvement loop.

astra-6.text:
What I find exciting is the possibility of using AI to improve the algorithms and infrastructure that AI itself depends on. You can imagine a system proposing a change, testing it, measuring whether it actually makes things faster or more efficient, and then building on the changes that work.

That feedback loop is really powerful. In areas where you can objectively evaluate an answer, you can search for solutions that a human engineer might never think to try. And even a small efficiency improvement can matter enormously when you apply it across large-scale training or inference.

The longer-term question is how far that can go. Could these systems help us discover fundamentally better learning algorithms? That’s a much harder challenge, but it’s the possibility I find most exciting: AI becoming a useful partner in the science of AI itself.

r001.rationale: It describes AI improving the algorithms and infrastructure it depends on, with a system proposing, testing, and building on successful changes—communicating iterative self-improvement in AI systems.

sol-6.1.text:
What excites me is the possibility of using AI to improve the building blocks of AI itself. There are so many choices involved in training a system—algorithms, optimization methods, how you use the hardware—and we can’t explore all of those possibilities by hand.

With something like AlphaEvolve, you can propose a change, test it, and use that feedback to search for something better. The crucial thing is having a reliable way to evaluate whether it really is better. When you have that, you can sometimes discover solutions that are quite surprising, things a human wouldn’t naturally think to try.

And then there’s a potential compounding effect: better algorithms make our systems more efficient, which lets us do more experiments, which may help us discover better algorithms again. That’s a very exciting feedback loop, although making it work across the full complexity of AI research is still a big challenge.

r001.rationale: The response describes an iterative feedback loop for improving AI algorithms and efficiency, but does not identify the improvement as occurring on the programming side of AI systems.
